Alfred North Whitehead was born in Ramsgate, Kent, England, in 1861, and was educated at Sherborne before attending Trinity College, Cambridge, where he studied mathematics. He earned his B.A. in 1884, and later collaborated with Bertrand Russell on the seminal work, *Principia Mathematica* (1910–1913).
After moving to the United States in 1924 to join Harvard University, Whitehead turned his focus to philosophy, where he published *The Concept of Nature* (1920) and his most significant work, *Process and Reality* (1929). His philosophy, which is known as "process philosophy," rejected the idea of irreducible brute matter, instead positing that reality is composed of interrelated, dynamic "occasions of experience." He is also known for his concept of "prehension" as a form of perception, applicable to both conscious and unconscious entities.
